title: David Loy's Response
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett suggests that Buddhist practice is not just about personal awakening, but also about responding to the challenges of the world in an authentic way. This requires finding a balance between cultivating one's own inner peace through meditation and engaging with social and ecological issues, while also embracing uncertainty and taking action without attachment to specific outcomes. By doing so, we can develop a sense of courage, humility, and openness that allows us to respond to the world's challenges in a meaningful way.

sentences.text: It's a big effort and a big production to create our sesshin practice.
This morning, I was actually really appreciating the difficulty of sesshin.
It's sort of complicated, uncomfortable, and dense.
You feel like you're squashed in here; we Americans like big open spaces, so being squashed in together is a lot.
There are so many ways you can do it wrong, and my body was a little uncomfortable this morning, making it hard to get out of bed.
It occurred to me that this is really good.
Within a safe, supportive situation, we can actually practice being in difficulty, a little bit of discomfort, a little bit of not my preference.

Is it possible for us to be in a situation that we're not completely enamored of all the details of, and just sit there right in the middle of that with a little curiosity, with maybe a little kindness?
We can wonder if our opinions are really right—whether the window should be open or closed, or whatever it is that the mind is fixating on and noticing.
We can really notice the power of judgmental thinking and internal complaining.
It's pretty funny, isn't it?
If you look at your mind, it's ridiculously prissy and picky.

Of course, within the context of having set aside these four days and choosing to come here, and mapping it as a great thing—a religious opportunity or a spiritual thing, or at least maybe I can work on my meditation and stress reduction—we kind of just see it as part of the price.
We put up with that because it'll probably feel better later.
That was my experience, and yours too; after breakfast, it was much more comfortable.
I like that.
But actually, our judgmental, picky mind is not so funny writ large in the world beyond the meditation hall.
It leads us to all kinds of difficulties, judgments, and harm—harm for ourselves and others.

I had the idea that being uncomfortable in the sesshin container is actually really good political work for us to deal a little more directly and honestly with our mind, to soften up a little bit around all that, to recognize that we don't have to let it run us.
We can view it with a little humor, with a little less attention.
So I think it's good for us.
The sesshin leaders will continue to do their best not to make it difficult; that's not difficult on purpose.
What I realize is that the sesshin leadership isn't just in a purpose of tweaking and refining, which we are constantly doing.
We have many meetings, and we are always trying to refine and improve the sesshin experience for everybody, making it smoother.
But I realize the purpose of that is not so that we'll all be comfortable.
The purpose of that is because that's our practice.
Our practice is to take good care of the sesshin and take good care of each other.
We probably will have failed if it suddenly gets all comfortable.
I don't know how that's even possible—like a waterbed, soft food, nice music, I don't know how that would work.
At the same time that the mind can be so pushed around by these little judgments and little niggles, it can also be so awestruck by the beauty of all this.
Funny little things catch your eye.
I noticed just now that Ken and Anne are relatively new to running the orchestra over here.
I noticed that they have the little books that tell them what to do carefully arranged on the exact same page for the next service.
It's just a beautiful sense of preparation and order, and we know what we're doing; it's just beautiful.
Maybe after your shoulders hurt for a couple of hours, you appreciate things like that more.
Anyway, I just want to say a few words in favor of difficulty when we have enough support to be mindful in that difficulty, when we can learn from it.
We probably can only do that together; this wouldn't work so well on our own.
Speaking of how these difficulties manifest in the world, I had a completely different talk in mind, which Jeff and I agreed to.
But then Norman Fischer, my teacher, sent a bunch of us a talk by David Loy that he gave last week in his home sangha in Boulder, Colorado.
It just seems like a really important talk, so I'm going to share that instead.
With all of David Loy's words, I'll try not to jump in too much with my own comments because I'll let his stand on their own, and I'll say a few things at the end.

It has been two weeks today since the election, and many of us are still in a state of shock, traumatized, disheartened, if not depressed, angry, fearful, and somewhat confused, wondering what's going to come next and wondering if there might be some silver lining to what's happening.
My response today is two parts.
First, I'd like to identify a very real silver lining, or at least the possibility of a silver lining, depending on how we respond to the situation.
Then, I'd like to say a bit about what I think is the most important contribution of Buddhist teaching to the situation, which can help us respond to it.
Let's begin with his end story.
A student asks the master, "In times of great difficulty, when times of great difficulty come, how should we meet them?"
And the answer is, "Welcome."
This path we're on is not about avoiding difficulties.
That doesn't mean passively accepting those difficulties when they present themselves, but it does mean engaging with them, not trying to avoid them.
Another story is also relevant here.
The student asks the master, "What is the constant activity of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
In other words, what is it that awakened people do all the time?
What's special about the way they live moment by moment?"
The answer from the master is, "An appropriate response."
In one way that seems simple, but in another way it's not.
Because in order to know how to respond appropriately, we have to understand the situation we're in.
There are different ways of understanding a situation, many different perspectives.
One of them is how short term or long term, how closely we are looking at the situation, and how much we can step back from it and take a larger perspective.
Here's a silver lining I'm wondering about.
Again, I'm not saying it's definitely a silver lining, but there's a possibility.
Is the distress we're feeling now opening up a new potential?
That's exactly what's needed.

I have to immediately qualify that because as an older, white, heterosexual male, there are certain types of anxiety that I'm probably not going to have to worry about compared to many women, gay people, people of color, or immigrants.
I acknowledge that, and yet, again, I am in a very privileged situation.
There are other important issues here too, other aspects to our distress that need to be emphasized and even appreciated.
Perhaps the shock of this election may also help us wake up.
You will remember that Hillary ran her campaign basically on the status quo, more of the same.
From what I can see, that is why she lost, because for an awful lot of people in the country, that's not what they wanted.
Among other things, the Democrats have controlled the presidency for sixteen of the last twenty-five years, and the gap between rich and poor during that time has accelerated rapidly.
So much for the party of the working class.
How much has the election of Donald Trump shaken us up?
Maybe in the process, it is waking us up in a way that the election of Hillary Clinton would not have done.

I'm struck by something that the philosopher provocateur, Slavoj Žižek—I think it's the same guy I've seen on YouTube, so you can see this guy say this if you want—says: "The real calamity is the status quo.
The real calamity is the status quo."

In which case, if people are responding, showing their dissatisfaction with the status quo, even if they are doing it for different reasons than I do, is that expression of dissatisfaction actually what's needed?
The response can be understood in many ways.
Let me share with you the way that stands out most for me right now.
Here are a few sentences by James Gustav Speth from a book he published back in two thousand eight, which means he wrote a written list in two thousand seven.
Keep that in your mind when you listen.
He wrote: "Half of the world's tropical and temperate forests are now gone.
The rate of deforestation in the tropics continues at about an acre per second, as it has for decades.
Half the planet's wetlands are gone.
An estimated ninety percent of large predator fish are gone.
Seventy-five percent of marine fisheries are overfished or fished to capacity.
Almost half of the corals are gone or seriously threatened.
Species are disappearing at rates about a thousand times faster than normal.
The planet hasn't seen such a spasm of extinction in sixty-five million years since the dinosaurs disappeared."
And more recently, a week or so ago, it was announced that from nineteen seventy to two thousand twenty, a short fifty-year period, two-thirds of all the wild animals on the planet have disappeared.
Maybe it means mammals.
Some years ago, E.O.
Wilson, a biologist, predicted by the end of the century half of the Earth's species, planet and animal, may be extinct or so weakened that they'll disappear soon thereafter.
Back to Speth now.
Desertification claims a Nebraska-sized area of productive capacity each year globally.
Persistent toxic chemicals can now be found by the dozens, and essentially each and every one of us.
Back to David Loy.

Something else I recently came across is that in the last forty years, that is to say in the lifetime of almost all of us here, about one-third of the world's cropland has been abandoned because of soil erosion or in other ways being unusable.
All we have to do, continues Speth, to destroy the planet's climate and biota and leave a ruined world to our children and grandchildren is to keep doing exactly what we're doing.

With no growth in human population or the world economy, just continue to generate greenhouse gases at current rates, just continue to impoverish ecosystems and release toxic chemicals at current rates.
The world in the latter half of this century won't be fit to live in.
But human activities are not holding at current levels; human activities are accelerating dramatically.
I wrote this back in two thousand seven.
Did you notice that just last week it was announced that this will be the third year in a row that set a new record as the warmest year in recorded history?
If all this is true, we need to wake up.
We need to wake up in a way that we haven't yet.
Why haven't we?
What does it take to wake us up?
In response to this, you might say that Hillary, unlike Donald Trump, acknowledged climate change and intended to do something about it, but given her public record, how much was she prepared to do?
The analogy that comes to my mind is that we're all in a big bus, a bus that's hurtling very, very fast towards a precipice.
We don't know what lies over that precipice.
We don't know if it's a sudden drop or a bumpy collapse, but we have good reason to suspect it's a very long way down.
People were fighting for the steering wheel of that bus.
One person wanted to speed up, stomp on the accelerator and go faster because he's not concerned; apparently, he doesn't believe there is a precipice.
But what about the other person?
Was she determined to stop the bus?

Maybe she would have slowed it down a little bit, maybe turn the wheel a bit, but it seemed to me that neither of our two main political parties is interested in acknowledging the crisis in a way that needs to be acknowledged.

I'm reminded of the Louisiana populist Huey Long, who put it very well: "Your government is like a restaurant, a restaurant with Republican waiters on one side and Democratic waiters on the other side.
No matter which set of waiters brings you your food, the legislative grub is all prepared in the same Wall Street kitchen.
The legislative grub is from the same Wall Street kitchen."
Suppose Hillary had won as expected, would we have all sat back on the bus more comfortably?
If Trump had been defeated, would that have encouraged us to become or remain more comfortable?
I think you can see what I'm getting at here.
The other side of this question that constantly comes back to me is a question for myself as it is for anyone else: Why is it so difficult for us to respond in the way that seems to be necessary?
The answer it seems to me is that for most of us, our concern is not generated by personal discomfort.
If you look at the history of the French Revolution or the Russian Revolution, the people who revolted did so because they were desperate.
Because they really had no choice.
Because they had to put their lives on the line.
Let's be honest.

For most of us here in the Bellingham bubble—because they're in the town of Bellingham, but I realize Bellingham bubble is equally true in alliterative, so I'll change that one word—for how many of us here in the Bellingham bubble is life essentially pretty comfortable?
When you look at your lives historically or geographically, we are incredibly privileged.
We are the most fortunate generation in human history when you consider the levels of disposable income, medical care, freedom, and just the ability to do what we want.

Or you can look at it geographically in contemporaneous terms of what's going on in the rest of the world, and you come to the same conclusion: how incredibly fortunate and how extraordinarily comfortable we are compared to life for the vast majority of people on the planet.
This is not a criticism; it's just a statement.
I'm talking about myself here as well.
How incredibly fortunate and how extraordinarily comfortable we are compared to life for the vast majority of people on the planet.
Not a criticism, a statement.

And I'm talking about myself here, about how difficult this is going to be for us to generate the level of passion and concern and response that's necessary if we're going to leave a decent planet for our descendants and for the other species on the Earth.
Because we're all in this bubble together, it's very hard not to take that for granted and just assume that's the way things are.
We need to remember that the kind of life that we now enjoy, our great-great-grandchildren are not going to have that kind of life.
The Bellingham bubble is a bubble; it will be popped.
The quality of life here that for no to no extent we can't help but take for granted that's not going to go on forever.
It's important for us, rather than simply enjoying our comforts until the bubble pops, to actually respond to this new challenge as much as we can, and to respond now.

That's the sense in which some kind of discomfort and anxiety and trauma that some of us are experiencing in one way or another during these last weeks might become something positive, encouraging us to see the sense of community that has been forming within some groups, people bonding together in a way that is needed if we're going to be able to respond appropriately to the kind of difficulties we can expect.
So please let's reflect on this.
My concern is that those of us who feel momentarily moved to do something will over time, being surrounded by other people who are not so moved, lose the energy and slip back into old ways.
And more familiar lifestyle habits.

I think we have to be careful and ask ourselves whether we are doing that and really try to help each other rise to the particular kind of challenge that this is, rather than seeing it as a temporary difficulty that we can adjust to or endure.
To some extent, our practice can encourage that.
Although it is possible to use our meditation practice, our Buddhist practice, as a kind of refuge from all this.
I'm concerned that we Buddhists may have discovered our own solution to the climate crisis and other ecological and social crises.
When we read something of the sort that I mentioned earlier, quoting Speth, we do become anxious.
But hey, we're Buddhist practitioners.
We know what to do when we're anxious, right?
Sit, facing the wall for a while, let go of our thoughts and feelings, and then we feel better.
That's maybe one kind of Buddhist response.
But not the kind of response that I'm talking about.
The second thing I want to talk about is perhaps the most important thing that Buddhism has to offer at this particular point: the Bodhisattva path.
The most essential thing about the Bodhisattva path is that the Bodhisattva has a double practice, a two-sided, two-faceted practice.
On the one hand, here she continues to work for their own awakening.

They continue their meditation and so forth; they work on their self-transformation and therefore and thereby realize or get in touch with that dimension or perspective in which nothing actually is missing, in which nothing is lacking, no better, no worse, nothing to gain.
To be able to touch that, and they also realize that that dimension by itself is insufficient; it's one-sided.
That it's important for us to ground ourselves in meditative equanimity, and then we talk about realizing emptiness.
And it's important that that grounding enables us or invigorates us to engage more compassionately, more wholeheartedly, in social and ecological activities.
And on the other hand, it's just as important for activists to have a meditative practice because otherwise it's very, very difficult to avoid getting frustrated, burned out, angry, and despairing.
I spent a lot of time recently talking to many Buddhist groups about how important it is to be socially and ecologically engaged.
And I'm reminded of my all-time favorite quotation by Nisargata.
Nisargata points this out very well: *When I look inside and see that I am nothing, that's wisdom.
When I look outside and see that I am everything, that's love.
When I look inside and see that I am nothing, that's wisdom.
When I look outside and see that I am everything, that's love.
And between the two, life moves.
Between the two, life moves.* More things about the Bodhisattva path could be mentioned here.
Traditionally, one of the most important things would be nonviolence, consistent with the first Buddhist precept that we don't injure living beings.
Along with that, the idea of non-polarization, which seems especially important now.

By non-polarization, I mean not objectifying or feeling separate from other people who have different ideas, people that we're trying to convince or struggling with, and not to label them as evil or different.
From a Buddhist perspective, we're not in a struggle of good against evil, but on a path that transforms delusion into wisdom, ignorance into awakening.
And that involves recognizing how we are all a part of this.
We are all complicit within the webs of delusion such as this election demonstrated.
It's very heartening to see the resistance that's already starting to catalyze.

I'm sure most of you heard about the incident that happened a few days ago at the Broadway show Hamilton in New York, where Vice President-Elect Pence was booed by many of the audience, and following the performance, some of the cast were on stage to make a statement.
I think we're going to see a lot more of that.
My sense is we're going to see the strongest resistance movement since the Vietnam War, maybe since the Civil War.

But what isn't clear yet is whether this kind of movement is going to bring us together in response to what's happening or are we going to create a growing gap between the people who are appalled by what Trump's election represents and the people who elected him.
Are we going to see greater and greater division or are we going to accept that despite the fact that we have different ideas and a different understanding, we're all responding to pain?
Everyone is suffering.
Will we be able to find ways to communicate to actually relate to them rather than deepening the chasm between us?
There are other things the Bodhisattva path emphasizes, such as pragmatism and skillful means.
This highlights the importance of creativity.
But I want to focus on what may be the most important thing: the Bodhisattva acts without attachment to the fruits of action.
This is really important and also potentially dangerous if we misunderstand it because it can encourage or rationalize a kind of half-hearted commitment.
We might decide, however, that we need to help convert a fossil fuel plant into renewable energy.
We work hard for a little while, but it doesn't seem to be happening.
And we say, "Oh well, I tried.
It isn't happening.
I'm not attached to results.
Back to the cushion."
It says in your laughter, I guess they laughed when you said that.
Maybe they had something like that going on in Boulder.
Is that the kind of non-attachment to the fruits of action that we need?
No.
I see that's a misunderstanding of what non-attachment means.
One way to make this point is to emphasize the distinction between a hundred-yard dash and a marathon.
When you're running a hundred-yard dash, the only thing that counts is getting you the goal line as quickly as possible.
You don't have to think of anything else.
But you don't run a marathon in that way.
If you do, you're going to exhaust yourself too quickly.
In order to run a marathon, yes, you are running.
You're not just sitting by the side, and you're moving in a certain direction.
At the same time, you're going in that direction one step at a time.
Just one step at a time.
Just this.
Just this.
One step at a time.
Nonetheless, a marathon is only twenty-six miles or so, and even if you're quite slow, even if you walk it, you're going to be able to finish it, probably finish it within a day.
But what about the actual situation we're faced with today, where we don't know how far the goal is, the goal line is, or how long it will take us to get there?
Or we have to be in it for the really, really long haul, which is more discouraging or intimidating in the sense that we don't know what or where the goal is, or even if there is a finish line.
And here I'm reminded of something that's recited in Zen centers every day: the four Bodhisattva vows.
The first of which is pertinent: Beings are numberless.
How to save them all?
Liberate them all.
Help them all.
Realize their true nature.

Because one is taking a vow to do something that actually can't be done; they can't be fulfilled in any measurable way, making it a goal-less kind of goal, which means that it's not about achieving a particular goal.
It's about a fundamental reorientation in the meaning of one's life, away from our usual preoccupation with our own comfort and our own separate well-being.
The vow is a commitment to transform and to transform our habits.
No, the fundamental meaning of my life is working for the well-being of everyone.
To remind ourselves of that, you could call that a goal, you could call it an attachment if you like, but it's something different.
It's really a transformation at the core that cuts through our usual self-preoccupation.

And the reason I emphasize that is that if you think about what a vow really means and take it seriously, you're not going to be intimidated by the comparatively minor task of working with others to save global civilization from destroying itself.
Laughter.
That's your cue.
The point is whether or not we become terribly discouraged, we still don't stop.
We get on with it.
Does this bodhisattva commitment and activity become the only game in town as the meaning of one's life?
I think it's not a vow that many of us can embody very successfully unless we're supported by meditation practice or some spiritual practice.
However, that still doesn't get at the most important thing that we need to say about what it means to act without attachment to the results of the action.
What pushes me in this direction is that some scientists may be saying, among themselves, behind closed doors at least, it may be too late.
Well, what if it is too late?
First question, too late for what?
Too late to avoid a breakdown of the kind of global civilization we've achieved in these last generations?
As Paul Ehrlich put it, in pushing other species to extinction, we're busy sawing off the limb on which we perch anyway.
Quite ironic, isn't it, that we've achieved a truly global civilization, and it may be that it's just busy destroying itself.
I'm not a scientist and I'm not in a position to offer any authoritative judgment on this matter, but scientists seem very concerned about what they are calling tipping points.
For example, the fact that the Arctic ice is melting more quickly than expected.
Without the white ice, the ocean absorbs more heat, which causes the ice to melt more and so forth.
Another example is methane gas, which is much more potent than carbon dioxide.
I've read there are approximately four hundred billion tons of methane frozen in the bottom of the Arctic in the Antarctic Ocean and buried in the permafrost, and both of these are now melting.
So we may be getting into a positive feedback loop, positive in the sense that the problem aggravates and escalates itself, not positive like what we want.
So, is it maybe too late?
So what does that mean?
We just don't know, do we?
The extra problem with that, of course, is that normally there's something paralyzing about not knowing.
It makes us freeze.
It's scary that we don't even know what's happening right now and we don't have any idea what's likely to happen or what's possible.
We just don't know.
But here we have something else to offer.
In Zen, don't know mind is an essential aspect of realization and practice.
Enlightenment or awakening isn't about suddenly thinking, "Oh, now I get it, everything in the world is this way, and that's why it's all happening."
It's just the opposite.
It's opening up to a deep don't know mind.
Bernie Glassman, the founder of the Zen Peacemakers, made this the first of his three principles: don't know mind.
And for practitioners, there's something invigorating about don't know mind.
One of my teachers, Robert Aitken, said, "Our task isn't about clearing up the mystery, but rather making the mystery clear.
Our task isn't about clearing up the mystery, but making the mystery clear."
When we open up to what's actually happening, we open up to a world that's fundamentally mysterious, and essential to that mystery is how little we actually know.
But that doesn't stop us from acting.

When we're open to our practice, when we return to the source, it's not about grasping that ground to cling to it or rest on it, indifferent to what's happening in the world, but to be taken by it, to give ourselves to it, and to find ourselves manifesting something greater than our egos.
We become a vehicle of something greater than ourselves.
We become instruments of that source.
And that means our job is to respond appropriately to whatever situation arises as best we can.
What that implies, I think, is this: our task is to do the very best we can not knowing if anything we do is going to make any difference.
To do the best we can not knowing if anything we do is going to make any difference.
That's an important part of what don't know mind means.
We don't know if what we do is important, but it's very important that we do it because it's what we are here for, and what we find ourselves called to do.
Again, I think we can only do this with the support of spiritual practice, and we know in our Zen practice that meditation is deeply helpful.

Bringing us back to that two-sided practice I was referring to earlier, we're able to ground ourselves in the equanimity, in the emptiness, in the fundamental perspective, the felt understanding that nothing is lacking.

Then we can act in the world in ways that are becoming necessary, with non-attachment, walking step by step, moment by moment, in the direction that's needed as part of a fundamental reorientation of what it means to be a practitioner living in the world, in a world that's changing so quickly.
And doing the very best we can, joyfully, without knowing if anything's going to make any difference, we don't know, and that is okay.
Knowing is not part of our job description.
There's a famous Jewish saying in the Perki Avot, which says something like, *It's not your responsibility to finish the work of healing the Earth.
Neither are you free to desist from it.* So it's not our responsibility, but it is.

Let me conclude this is the end of David Loy by saying that if we're not able to respond in these ways, we still understand our practice only as a refuge, simply as a way of taking care of ourselves, avoiding the great challenge we're faced with, then maybe Buddhism isn't what's needed.

But I think this is exactly why and where Buddhism is so important because it can teach us that our engagement with the world is not a distraction from our practice, but an essential part of our practice.
So, powerful words from David Loy.
Add a little bit, and we'll close and continue this endless task.

Like our other essential offering, and he mentioned this about not objectifying others, but it goes deeper than that, I think, to really understand the mind more deeply, and to question and understand and transcend our habitual dualistic thinking.
You know, it's so automatic in us: I like it, I don't like it.
I'm me, you're you.
It should be this way, or it should be that way.
You're a Trump supporter, or you're not.
We've solved so easily into these this or that ways of thinking.

I think we have a deep task because we have been so fortunate as to have the luxury and the support and the teachings of this way, that it's our job to really live a softer, more curious, more flexible life based not on dualistic thinking.
Not that we are going to run around reaching at people as, "Dualistic thinking, you bozo," right?
That won't help; it's in fact dualistic.
But can we live this?
Can we be living examples?

I think everything David Loy said is a manifestation of that: living examples of people who are doing our best to soften our way through dualism into the deeply connected nature of all that is, what Tidna Han calls interbeing.
And can we do this in a way that's strong and humble?
We have to put some things together that we don't put together because dualistic thinking blocks us.
Can we be strong and humble?
Can we be sure and curious?
Can we be energetic and really listening?
Put your own together because it really does seem like it's true what he's saying about the bus.
It's not so good to plunge over the edge with the whole planet and our Bellingham bubble.
And actually it might be in terms of climate change that Bellingham is the best bubble around, better than Boulder.
They've got massive problems with wildfires and their water supply is partially glacial, and we're just getting more, you know, plenty of rain.
We're getting a nicer climate actually, more in the winter, that's nice, you know, a little drier in the summer.
We like climate change here.
Well, it's hard to bring us down, but I think that's what we've got to do.
Thank you for everybody for beginning our sesshin together, being curious in the middle of our discomfort and confusions and room rearranging and figuring out how to do this together.
We do pretty well, and most importantly, we do pretty well together.
So thanks for being part of the together part.

verbatim.text: Well, it's a big effort and a big production to create our sesshin practice. And this morning I was actually, it's going to sound funny, but I was actually really appreciating the difficulty of sesshin. You know, it's sort of complicated and uncomfortable and sort of dense. You know, you feel like sort of squoze in here, like we like, we're Americans, we like big open spaces, squoze in here together. With all these ways you can do it wrong. And my body was a little uncomfortable this morning and it was hard to get out of bed. And it somehow occurred to me that this is really good. That within a safe, supportive situation, we can actually practice, like being in difficulty, a little bit of difficulty,

a little bit of discomfort, a little bit of not my preference. You know, like is it possible for us to be in a situation that we're not completely enamored of all the details of and just sit there right in the middle of that, you know, with a little curiosity, with maybe a little kindness, a little wondering if our opinions are really right, that the window should be open or closed or whatever it is that the mind is fixating on and noticing, you know, like really noticing the power of judgmental thinking and internal complaining. And it's pretty funny, you know, isn't it? If you look at your mind, it's pretty funny how ridiculously prissy we are, you know, picky. And of course, within the context of having set aside these four days and chosen to come here

and mapping it as a great thing, a religious opportunity or a spiritual thing, or at least maybe I can work on my meditation and stress reduction, I think we kind of just see it as part of the price, you know what I mean? Well, I'll put up with that because it'll probably feel better later. And that was my experience, yours too. After breakfast, much more comfortable. I like that. But actually, of course, our judgmental, picky mind is not so funny, writ large in the world, beyond the meditation hall. Leads us to all kinds of difficulties and judgments and harm, harm for ourselves and others.

So, I don't know, I had the idea that being uncomfortable in the Sachine container is like actually really good political work for us to deal a little more directly and honestly with our mind, to soften up a little bit around all that, to recognize that we don't have to let it run us.
